amendments.rule: A Greek article governing an expressed vocative is `aligned` to the address word the ASV supplies for it — *ye*, *thou*, *O* — headed on that word, and the noun it governs stands bare. `Οἱ ἄνδρες` → *Ye husbands* gives *Ye* to the article and *husbands* to `ἄνδρες`, as EPH.6.4 → *ye fathers*, EPH.6.9 → *ye masters*, the three articles of REV.18.20 and REV.19.5 → *all ye his servants* do, and as an article taking a supplied *O* does at REV.6.10 and REV.12.12. This is rules 51 and 60's argument for a third kind of supplied word: a slot the ASV fills in front of the noun and no other source token competes for is the article's own to take, and an address word is such a filler. REV.19.5 is what shows that rule 20 is not the contrast — the possessive slot there is already occupied by `αὐτοῦ` → *his*, and the article still takes *ye* — because an address word is not a determiner a genitive pronoun can displace. Rule 23 is the contrast, and the test is the ASV's: where it writes a bare vocative and supplies no word at all the article realizes nothing, as `οἱ οἰκέται` → *Servants* at 1PE.2.18, `Οἱ ἄνδρες` → *Husbands* at EPH.5.25 and EPH.5.28, and EPH.6.1 and EPH.6.5 do. Where the Greek vocative is anarthrous no article competes and the supplied word is an ordinary rule 7 helper on the noun: `γυναῖκες` → *ye wives*, `Φιλιππήσιοι` → *ye Philippians*, `οὐρανέ` → *thou heaven*, `Κορίνθιοι` → *O Corinthians*. REV.18.20 writes both halves in one verse, which is what shows that the presence of the article and not English word order decides. The corpus has no unit anywhere in which an article stands before a noun whose English carries a supplied address word and is left `unrepresented`. Where a participle rather than a noun follows, rule 32 splits the unit as it always does and the article keeps only the address word. That closing clause reaches only an article the ASV writes the address word **for**, and which article that is is decided by the token the address word stands in front of, never by the mere presence of an article somewhere in the vocative phrase. An article standing in that phrase but governing something other than the addressed noun is not that noun's article and takes no address word. Where the ASV writes the address word on an **expressed anarthrous** vocative noun under this rule's anarthrous arm and a further article governs a participle or a phrase standing in **apposition** to that noun, the noun has already written the antecedent, so rule 32's apposition clause empties the article and the participle keeps the supplied relativizer along with its own verb: `ὁδηγοὶ τυφλοί, οἱ λέγοντες` → *ye blind guides, that say* gives the discontinuous *ye … guides* to `ὁδηγοί`, a bare *blind* to the adjective, nothing to the article, and *that say* to the participle, as `Ἰερουσαλὴμ Ἰερουσαλήμ, ἡ ἀποκτείνουσα` → *O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that killeth* leaves its article empty with *O … Jerusalem* on the first name. Rule 31's expressed-head-noun test reaches the same answer, the addressed noun being an expressed head noun standing in front of the article, so the two tests agree and neither is a licence to hand such an article a second address word the ASV never wrote. A reference comparison will report such an `unrepresented` article as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction.
amendments.why: Rule 89's closing sentence — that where a participle follows, the article keeps the address word — reads as reaching any article in a vocative phrase followed by a participle, and MAT.23 met that configuration three times with the address word already on an expressed anarthrous vocative noun (23:16, 23:24, 23:37). There rules 31 and 32 empty the article and the noun takes the *ye* or *O*, which is what those three verses did and what 23:37 corroborates by aligning the genuinely substantival τούς to *them* in the same verse. The amendment scopes the closing clause to an article the ASV actually writes an address word for and states the apposition case in terms, rather than leaving the over-broad sentence in place with a cross-reference. It adds no empirical claim: rule 89's own anarthrous arm, rule 32's apposition clause and rule 31's expressed-head-noun test all already give this answer, and the BSB reports on 23:16 οἱ and 23:37 ἡ are the disagreements rule 32 says are not corrections.

conventions: An article standing after an expressed anarthrous vocative and governing a participle in apposition to it is `unrepresented`, and the supplied address word rides on the vocative noun under rule 89's anarthrous arm: 23:16 and 23:24 hodegoi typhloi, hoi legontes / hoi diylizontes -> *ye blind guides, that say* and *that strain out*, and 23:37 Ierousalem Ierousalem, he apokteinousa -> *O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that killeth*. Rule 89's closing clause about a following participle reaches only an article the ASV writes the address word for; rules 31 and 32 empty this one, and 23:37 confirms the line by aligning tous before apestalmenous to *them* in the same verse. BSB reports 23:16 hoi and 23:37 he as represented, and that is not a correction.

epano autou is one `aligned` unit on *thereon* headed on the pronoun at 23:20 and 23:22, where the ASV writes one solid word, and splits at 23:18 into to -> *that*, epano -> *is upon*, autou -> *it*, where it writes four. The count of English words decides (rules 35, 81, 94); the identical Greek phrase read two ways in one chapter is rule 24's habit and not an inconsistency to level. 23:21 auton -> *therein* takes the whole solid word on the pronoun though no preposition is expressed, rule 106's accusative arm having no separate particle to place.

report: Read all 54 candidate groups and the dump end to end. No cross-verse split found, so patches is empty.

The article (110 occurrences, 14 treatments) resolves on three lines the chapter holds without exception: rules 21/23, aligned where the ASV writes a determiner and unrepresented where it writes none (23:5, 6, 7, 13, 15, 22, 23 six times, 28, 33); rules 20/57, emptied where a possessive or an English 's occupies the slot (23:1, 2, 3, 4 twice, 5 twice, 8, 9, 30, 32, 34, 37, 38); rules 31/32 by the expressed-head-noun test, unrepresented at 23:16, 17, 19, 24, 37 and pronoun-taking at 23:13, 20, 21, 22, 31, 37, 39. 23:37 writes both arms of that last line in one verse, and both arms of rule 20/76 as well.

The group that most looks like a split is not one: epano autou is joined as *thereon* at 23:20 and 23:22 and split three ways at 23:18 (*that* / *is upon* / *it*). That is rule 94's count of English words, not two analyses; recorded as a convention so a later reader does not level it. Likewise en as *at*/*in*/*by*, exothen as *outside* (articular) against *outwardly* (bare adverb), hoti as *for*/*because*/*that*, and apo aligned at 23:35 but absorbed at 23:33 are all ASV-side differences.

The table is blind to `added`, so I checked the dump: the only two `added` units are the supplied appositional *even* at 23:9 (substantival-article carrier) and 23:10 (articular appositive), both on rule 105's article arm, and no supplied word of any other class is `added` anywhere. The folded supplied words - *these* 23:3, *so* 23:15, *some* 23:34 twice, the italic *is* 23:39, the address words, and the generic nominals *man*, *men*, *men's*, *things*, *matters* - each have a standing token that licenses them.

BSB: all ten disagreements are documented convention differences (rules 20, 21, 23, 32, 36, 70) and none is a genuine error. Rules 32 and 70 say in terms that such a report is not a correction. No accepted edge was touched.

Two units rest on analogy rather than attested precedent and are left as written, each already naming its competing reading in its note: 23:37 hon tropon as `noncompositional` on *even as* (rules 39 and 45 are scoped to a me-cluster and to a prepositional phrase, and a relative plus an accusative of manner is neither), and 23:21 auton as *therein* where rule 106's accusative arm has no separate particle to place. One instance each, no corpus row for tropos or for a bare accusative *therein* in the packet, so neither is promoted.
